question.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} - 5y = \cos 2x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\qquad$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155496/assets/db5806ea651ef0c5a635e5b019ad77c1dc4f93c3f8d7d0a9ae525669ff25c776.svg).

$\qquad$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x) =$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155496/assets/0c0a62974ee1a4d6b4f35b49f36d737cdb19a2190983bb28b55a74e01daae4d6.svg).

$\qquad$ Therefore, the particular solution is $y_p(x) =$  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155496/assets/55ecfbb20bb6e0166c9d676d9290c15c795ec855e2f171bc21b9df93c4bc497f.svg).
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution $y_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
y_c' - 5y_c = 0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c  = Ae^{5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable $y_p,$ we set $A = u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
y_p(x) = u(x)e^{5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of $y_p$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate $u'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{5x})}^{′}-5(u{e}^{5x}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+5u{e}^{5x}-5u{e}^{5x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}}-\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $y_p = u(x)e^{5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{5x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{5x} \\  & ={e}^{5x}\int {e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
